intro: Welcome to Ephesus. You are standing in the streets of a city in İzmir province whose story reaches back to the 10th century BC. This is one of the best-preserved Roman cities of antiquity — and just ahead waits the marble façade that made it famous: the Library of Celsus. Shall we begin?
history: The story of Ephesus begins with a goddess. When Ionian settlers founded the city, it grew around the Temple of Artemis. Then came Rome. Ephesus became capital of the province of Asia, home to over 200,000 people. So how did all this splendour end? Not with a battle, but quietly: silt crept into the harbour, the ships stopped coming, and the city slowly declined.
structure-1: You are now in front of the Library of Celsus. Look up at this marble façade. Most visitors take it for a library alone, but it is also the face of a tomb: Celsus' sarcophagus still lies in the chamber beneath the apse. The front you see was re-erected stone by stone in 1970-78. The model in the app shows it at its full height, and the hall behind it only as high as its walls survive.
structure-2: And here is the Great Theatre, one of the largest theatres of antiquity. Its three-tiered cavea is cut into the slope of Mount Pion, looking down the Harbour Street at a Roman stage building. Plays were not the only drama here: the riot of the silversmiths in the Acts of the Apostles took place on these very tiers. Pause for a moment and imagine thousands of voices rising at once.
structure-3: On the slope opposite Curetes Street stand the homes of the city's wealthiest: the Terrace Houses. Six luxury residences, their floors in mosaic and their walls in fresco. What astonishes most is the comfort — underfloor heating, enclosed drains, even glazed windows, all in the first century AD. Nowhere else shows so clearly what a rich Roman's house was actually like. In the model you can step inside one unit, around its colonnaded court.
structure-4: Now to the city's most sacred place: the Temple of Artemis, one of the Seven Wonders. Picture a marble forest 137 metres long, raised on marshy ground. Pliny tells us 36 of its columns were carved in relief at the base. Of that forest, a single column, re-erected from fragments, stands today. The model shows the third temple, rebuilt in the 4th century BC.
structure-5: Curetes Street is the main colonnaded street of Ephesus, running from the Library of Celsus to the theatre, lined with monuments and statues. As you walk these stones, think of the crowds who passed this way centuries ago.
facts: Did you know? The Temple of Artemis was one of the Seven Wonders; a single re-erected column remains today. The Great Theatre seated 24,000 people. According to Acts, the two-hour chant of 'Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!' against Saint Paul filled this very bowl. The Terrace Houses had underfloor and wall heating, enclosed drains and glazed windows — in the first century AD. And one last secret: Ephesus was a port. Silt from the Küçük Menderes filled the harbour, and today the sea lies 5 km from the ruins.
outro: This brings our journey through Ephesus to an end. Before you go, a small request: please leave the stones untouched, keep to the marked paths and carry water with you. These stones have waited for centuries; let them keep waiting for those who come after you. Enjoy your visit.
